title: Security & Compliance Integrated Playbook: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary:
This integrated playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's security and compliance controls for RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, Secure SDLC, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and the risk & exceptions process. It is intended for security, platform, infra, and product engineering teams responsible for designing, implementing, and operating production inference services.

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood cloud-hosted services and Private offering control plane components.
- Includes guidance for Dedicated customer environments where Redwood has operational responsibility.
- Does not replace customer-specific contractual obligations (see customer-specific addenda).

Owners and escalation:
- Primary owner: Security (security@redwood.example).
- Secondary owners: Eng-Infra (cloud accounts), Eng-SRE (observability & runbooks), Eng-Serving-Runtime (service-level controls).
- Escalation path: Service owner -> Eng-SRE on-call -> Security on-call -> CTO for high-impact incidents.

1) RBAC & Authentication
Principles:
- Principle of least privilege (PoLP) for humans and service identities.
- Role-based assignment with group membership managed in Okta (SSO).
- Use short-lived credentials and scoped service accounts for platform services.

Role definitions (examples):
- security-admin: full access to security tooling and evidence storage (restricted).
- infra-operator: manage cloud infra, terraform run privileges (audit-only changes required).
- service-owner: deploy and manage specific service stacks; no cross-service infra privileges.
- read-only-observability: access to dashboards/logs for troubleshooting without the ability to delete or export protected data.

Policy mapping and implementation:
- Human access: Okta groups mapped to cloud IAM roles (AWS IAM / GCP IAM). All privileged actions require 2FA + device posture check.
- Service-to-service: use short-lived workload identities (e.g., AWS STS or GKE Workload Identity).
- Secrets: store in HashiCorp Vault / cloud KMS. No plaintext secrets in repos or CI logs.

Access request & review procedure:
1. Employee requests access via internal access portal (link: /tools/access-requests).
2. Request includes business justification, owner approval, and duration (default 90 days for elevated roles).
3. Security performs risk review for privileged roles.
4. Quarterly access review: owners attest to membership lists; automated deprovisioning for stale accounts.

Automation & guardrails:
- Automated group-to-role sync jobs run nightly and log changes to the audit pipeline.
- Policy-as-code for IAM bindings stored in repo infra/iam with pull-request review required.

2) Audit Logging
Objectives:
- Ensure reliable capture of authorization, authentication, configuration changes, and privileged actions for forensic and compliance needs.
- Centralize logs in cloud logging + SIEM (Splunk/Chronicle) and retain per policy.

Log categories and retention:
- Authentication & SSO events: 1 year (default), 7 years for regulated customers.
- IAM policy changes and role bindings: 7 years (immutable archive).
- API access / service-level audit logs (create/update/delete): 1 year (hot), archived to cold storage for 7 years.
- Security alerts and incident artifacts: retain for 7 years.

Ingestion & pipeline:
- All service and cloud logs forwarded to the logging collector (fluentd/OTel) and routed to: SIEM (real-time analysis), cold S3/GCS bucket (encrypted, immutability flag set where required).
- SLA: log ingestion latency < 5 minutes for critical auth events; missing metrics trigger a page to Eng-SRE.

Alerting and monitoring:
- Pre-built detection rules: suspicious login locations, privilege escalation events, mass permission changes, failed auth spikes.
- Thresholds: e.g., > 10 failed root account attempts within 5 minutes => critical alert.

Example export command (AWS CloudTrail -> S3):
- aws cloudtrail create-trail --name redwood-infra-trail --s3-bucket-name redwood-audit-archive --is-multi-region-trail
- aws cloudtrail start-logging --name redwood-infra-trail

3) Data Residency & Retention
Data classification:
- Public: non-sensitive product docs, marketing. Retention: 1 year.
- Internal: internal docs, telemetry that is not PII. Retention: 3 years.
- Restricted: PII, customer data, model inputs flagged by customers. Retention: per contract; default 7 years for regulated workloads.

Residency controls:
- Default hosting regions: US (us-west-2), EU (europe-west1).
- Customer can request dedicated-region hosting; this must be captured in order provisioning and enforced via placement policies.
- Cross-region replication of restricted data is disabled unless explicitly approved and documented.

Retention schedules and enforcement:
- Retention policies are enforced via lifecycle rules for object stores and time-based deletion jobs for databases.
- Example S3 lifecycle rule: transition to Glacier after 90 days, expire after configured retention period.

Retention table (examples):
- Audit logs: hot 1 year -> cold archive 7 years.
- Backups of customer data: 90 days (default) or contract-specific.
- Telemetry (aggregated, non-PII): 3 years.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Software Development Lifecycle)
Goals:
- Reduce vulnerability surface via automated tooling and mandatory review gates.
- Ensure reproducible builds and traceable artifacts for compliance evidence.

Required controls:
- Repo protections: branch protections, required PR reviews (2 approvers for infra changes), status checks passing.
- CI pipeline gates: unit tests, linting, SAST (e.g., Semgrep), dependency checks (Snyk/Dependabot), license compliance checks.
- Secrets scanning: pre-commit and CI-level scanning (trufflehog, SOPS policy).
- Build reproducibility: deterministic build artifacts with provenance metadata stored in artifact registry (container image digest, SBOM).

PR checklist for production-impacting changes:
1. Design doc reference present and linked.
2. Threat model updated for changes to auth, data flow, or external dependencies.
3. Security scan results attached, with remediation plan for high/critical findings.
4. Rollback plan and runbook updated.

Deployment controls:
- Canary rollouts for infra and runtime changes by default (10% -> 50% -> 100%).
- Automatic rollback on error rate increase (predefined SLO breach).

5) Incident Response - Security Procedures
Severity classification (high level):
- Sev1 (Critical): Active compromise or data exfiltration affecting production or customer data.
- Sev2 (High): Service outage with security implications.
- Sev3 (Medium): Suspicious activity contained with limited impact.

Immediate triage checklist (first 30 minutes):
1. Triage owner declares severity and posts to incident channel (#inc-sevX).
2. Preserve volatile evidence: take memory snapshots (where applicable), clone affected instances, set fw rules to limit outbound traffic.
3. Capture timeline: record first observed, affected systems, indicators of compromise (IOCs).
4. Notify legal and PR for incidents with potential customer impact.

Forensic preservation commands (examples):
- Linux instance snapshot: aws ec2 create-image --instance-id i-12345678 --name "forensic-i-12345678-$(date +%Y%m%d)"
- Export audit logs to secure evidence bucket (write-once): aws s3 cp /var/log/auth.log s3://redwood-evidence-bucket/incidents/2026-xx-xx/ --storage-class DEEP_ARCHIVE --object-lock-mode GOVERNANCE

Post-incident activities:
- Root cause analysis and timeline within 7 business days.
- Security postmortem published (redacted as required) with action owners and due dates.
- Verify remediation and close with a remediation verification run.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows
Artifact catalog (minimum for audits like SOC2):
- Policies and control descriptions (this document + controlbook).
- Access lists and evidence of quarterly access reviews.
- Audit log exports, SIEM alert history, and detection tuning notes.
- Secure SDLC artifacts: design docs, PR history, build artifacts, SBOMs, vulnerability remediation tickets.
- Incident response artifacts: timelines, forensic captures, communications.

Evidence collection steps:
1. Evidence owner receives request via compliance tracker (link: /tools/compliance-tracker) and acknowledges within 2 business days.
2. Owner collects artifacts and uploads to the Evidence Vault (S3 bucket with restricted access and MFA delete).
3. Evidence is tagged with metadata: control-id, audit-id, date-range, owner.
4. Auditor access is read-only and time-boxed; all auditor sessions are logged.

Retention and attestations:
- Evidence retention follows the retention schedule in Section 3.
- Control owners must provide quarterly attestations with signed statements stored in the evidence vault.

7) Risk & Exceptions Process
When an exception is requested:
- Requestor completes the Risk Exception Request (RER) template with: scope, risk description, compensating controls, mitigation timeline, and owner.
- Security performs a risk assessment and assigns risk score (Likelihood x Impact).
- Approval matrix: 
  - Low risk: Security lead
  - Medium risk: Security + Eng-Infra manager
  - High risk: CISO + CTO + Legal
- Exceptions are time-limited (max 180 days) and require monitoring and a documented mitigation plan.

Monitoring for exceptions:
- Security sets up extra telemetry and weekly attestations for active exceptions.
- Exceptions are revisited in the monthly risk review board.

Appendices
A. Useful links:
- Access portal: /tools/access-requests
- Evidence Vault: s3://redwood-evidence-bucket/
- Compliance tracker: /tools/compliance-tracker
- Incident Slack channels: #inc-sev1, #inc-sev2, #sec-oncall

B. Example policy-as-code snippet (IAM binding YAML):
- resource: aws_iam_role
  name: service-owner-role
  properties:
    assume_role_policy: >-
      {
        "Version": "2012-10-17",
        "Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/infra-ci"}, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"}]
      }

This playbook is intended to be a living document. Owners must review it at least annually or after any major control change.
